history_of_present_illness:
Leprosy is a very chronic, almost incurable disease with a protracted incubation period of two to ten years, sometimes extending to twenty-seven years. It typically sets in with indefinite prodromata, including malaise, weariness, mental depression, and irregular febrile attacks (leprotic fever) associated with sweating and somnolence, which may be mistaken for malaria. Other early manifestations can include progressive weakness, alternating dryness and hypersecretion of the nasal mucous membrane with frequent epistaxis, neuralgic manifestations, paraesthesias, and headache. In nerve leprosy, vague signs of neuritis may precede definite symptoms.

The disease presents in two main types: nodular (skin, hypertrophic, or tubercular) and nerve (smooth, maculo-anaesthetic, or atrophic), with a mixed form combining features of both.

Nodular leprosy begins with an outbreak of brownish-red spots that later become pigmented and thickened. These erythematous spots, which come in crops with fever, range from 1 or 2 millimeters to palm-sized blotches. They are raised and preferentially appear on the lobes of the ears, nasal alae, forehead, eyebrows, cheeks, and chin, as well as the extensor surfaces of the forearms, thighs, and buttocks. The palms, soles, hairy scalp, groin, and axillary regions are almost never affected. Initially hyperaesthetic, these spots soon show loss of pain and temperature sense (dissociation of sensation) but retain touch, and they do not sweat. Successive febrile accessions lead to the development of reddish-brown, elastic, greasy nodular masses, often on the sites of the initial spots. These protruding nodules can give the face a leonine or satyriasis appearance. Hair falls out of the eyebrows and bearded regions. Nodules also develop in the mucous membranes of the nose, mouth, and larynx, causing fetid discharges, nasal obstruction, difficulty in mastication and breathing, and a raucous voice. Eye involvement is frequent, with infiltrations of the eyelids, conjunctivae, cornea, and iris, leading to ulcerations and loss of sight. Nodules may resolve but often ulcerate, leading to various contractures and deformities. The course is essentially chronic, often ending in cachexia in about ten years, with gradual temperature fall and somnolence.

Nerve leprosy's prodromal phase is marked by neuralgic pains and sensory disturbances (formication, paraesthesias) due to irritation of nerve fibers, particularly the ulnar, peroneal, and facial nerves, rarely extending above the knee or elbow. Early signs include anaesthesia in the region supplied by the ulnar nerve and contractures of the fourth and fifth fingers. Smooth, yellowish-brown spots may precede neuritis. Fully developed cases feature anaesthetic spots, trophic lesions of the skin and bone, and muscular palsies. These flat, sunburnt-colored spots are often single, 0.5 to several inches in diameter, do not sweat, and most frequently appear on covered parts of the body (trunk, buttocks, scapular region, thighs, arms). They may resemble ringworm but are oval with no scaling. Bullous eruptions, often around the knuckles, are rare but can lead to ulceration. Nerve trunks, especially the ulnar at the elbow and the great auricular, enlarge, appearing spindle-shaped or beaded. Initially tender, these enlargements later become painless, leading to extensive anaesthesia and trophic changes of the skin and nails of fingers and toes, such as felons, glazed skin, bullae (rupturing to form ulcers), and absorption of phalangeal bones (lepra mutilans). Perforating ulcers are common. Muscular palsies, atrophies, and contractures are more prevalent in the face and upper extremities, causing claw hand deformities (atrophy of thenar, hypothenar, and interossei muscles, with extension of the first joint and flexion of the two distal joints of the fingers). Wrist-drop is not uncommon, but foot-drop and Charcot's joint condition are rare. Paralysis of the orbicularis palpebrarum is common, and eye involvement (ectropion of the lower lid, corneal ulceration) occurs in about 45% of cases.
exposure_and_epidemiology:
Leprosy, caused by the acid-fast bacillus *Bacillus leprae* (discovered by Hansen in 1871), is believed to have originated in India (Rig Veda, 1400 B.C.) or Egypt (Ebers papyrus, 1300 B.C.), though the ancients likely confused it with other disfiguring diseases. It was introduced into Europe from Egypt in the first century B.C. by Pompey's legions and spread widely by the crusaders, leading to approximately 20,000 leper asylums in Europe by the 14th century. Drastic isolation measures led to its practical disappearance from Europe by the 15th century.

Geographically, leprosy has almost disappeared from Europe, with limited, diminishing cases in Norway and Sweden, an uncertain number in the Balkan region and Turkey, and some cases in Brittany, Provence, Portugal, and Spain. Africa is heavily infected, particularly Central and East Africa, with prevalence as high as one in four in parts of the Cameroons. Asia harbors many major centers, with vast numbers in China and India, about 100,000 lepers in Japan, and 3,000 in the Philippines. In the United States, cases significantly decreased from 278 in 1902 to 146 in 1912, concentrated around the Great Lakes, among Orientals on the Pacific Coast, and in the Gulf region (Louisiana and Florida). Hawaii had 696 lepers and Porto Rico 28. The disease is also found in South America (Columbia, Venezuela, Brazil), Mexico, Central America, Australia (Queensland, New South Wales), New Caledonia, and other Pacific islands.

Etiologically, *Bacillus leprae* morphologically and tinctorially resembles the tubercle bacillus. It is found in profusion within granulomatous tissue of the corium and subcutaneous structures of leprous nodules, mainly within "lepra cells," but also in endothelial and connective-tissue cells and free in lymphatic channels as "globi." Differentiation from *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* involves its presence in huge numbers, cigar-bundle-like packets, palisade groups (not chains), solid staining with coarser, widely separated granules, and its lesser resistance to decolorization with 3% HCl in alcohol (decolorizes in ~2 hours vs. 12-24 hours for TB). Crucially, *B. leprae* has not been surely cultivated or successfully inoculated with pathogenic results into guinea pigs or other experimental animals. It spreads primarily through lymphatics, but may enter the bloodstream during febrile accessions, and stains readily by Gram's method.

Epidemiologically, consensus suggests every case originates from direct or indirect contact, though proof of transmission and its exact manner are largely lacking. Arning's inoculation experiment on a condemned criminal in Hawaii (who had lepers in his family) is often cited but considered questionable, as numerous self-inoculation attempts by physicians (Danielson, Profeta) have been negative. Transmission to long-term attendants is rare (e.g., Father Damien), with hundreds working for years without contracting the disease. However, cases exist where close living contact (sharing a bed, clothes) led to infection. Even with intimate contact, infection rates are low (4.5% among healthy Hawaiians living with lepers, 9 out of 181 spouses). Data from Japan indicates children of lepers (7%) have a higher rate than spouses (3.8%) or housemates (2.7%). Evidence suggests infection is more prevalent in early life, similar to tuberculosis. The disappearance of leprosy following isolation in Europe (13th-14th centuries) and Norway supports its contagiousness, though Hansen's observation of no leprosy among descendants of Norwegian lepers in the U.S. might suggest other factors. It is generally held that children separated from leprous surroundings after birth are unlikely to develop the disease. Men are affected twice as often as women, possibly due to greater opportunities for contact.

No definite mode of transmission is known. While itch mites are unproven, leprosy bacilli have been found in the stomachs of flies feeding on leprotic ulcerations, suggesting flies might deposit bacilli on nasal orifices or wounds. Cockroaches have been found to harbor acid-fast rods for up to fourteen days after feeding on leprosy nodules, but bedbugs, head lice, and mosquitoes show little evidence of multiplication or prolonged carriage. Jonathan Hutchinson's theory of consumption of imperfectly cured fish is no longer supported. While the nasal mucosa, particularly ulcerations of the septum, were once considered the primary site of initial lesions and infection, few now believe it's a major transmission route, and nasal smears from close contacts are often negative. The long incubation period hinders understanding transmission. There's a growing belief that frequent use of soap and water may prevent infection, possibly through abraded skin. Sexual intercourse has been suspected but unproven as a transmission route.

Rat leprosy, caused by an almost identical organism, naturally occurs in rats (Stefansky, 1903), with two types: skin/muscle and lymphatic gland involvement, mimicking human leprosy pathology. Infection in rats occurs readily through skin abrasions or subcutaneous injection, but there's no evidence of insect involvement in rats. While prevalent globally, there seems to be no connection between rat and human leprosy.
